summary:
Caldas stands under the national framework of Colombia, where legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

The legal framework is assessed against a national pattern of lethal violence. Hate crimes killed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025. On 14 April 2025 national reporting described Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek, who died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon with no one arrested; her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023, with 41 trans women killed in 2023 and a further eight between February and April 2024.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Guajira, armed groups have circulated flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; armed groups gave trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. An activist quoted in the investigation states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings as ordinary cases.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

No finding specific to Caldas on law, enforcement practice or incidents affecting trans people appears in the sources available. The reporting carried here is national in scope or concerns other departments, and nothing in it marks Caldas as materially safer or more dangerous than the national picture.
tangentialFactors:
The killing that drew national attention occurred in Antioquia, a department that borders Caldas, and the organised "social cleansing" campaigns are documented in Caquetá and Guajira. Proximity to departments where armed groups issue kill lists is a turbulence factor rather than a finding about Caldas itself, since no source places such a campaign inside Caldas.

The gap between statute and street is the central comparative point. Colombia's identification rules, hate-crime framework and partner-recognition regime rank among the most developed in Latin America, yet the UN Independent Expert's May 2025 mission found institutional progress disconnected from daily lived experience, and killings continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

Recording practice weakens the protection machinery. An activist quoted in the Caquetá investigation states that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide as such, logging the killings as ordinary cases, which affects how quickly a visitor-facing threat would be classified and investigated.
